name: Seated cable row and chest-supported row
angleNote: Pull: 0% = arms straight (reaching to the pulley, or hanging), 100% = hands at the trunk. The trunk angle is held by the variant. Shoulder and elbow torques per arm, hip per side; drag the figure to turn it.

strength.note: Shoulder extension (positive) and flexion (negative) peak torque per arm, taken as constant across the range: Mayer's isometric means for men (93 and 68 Nm), measured standing.
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric)

strength.note: Horizontal abduction (positive: rear delts, with the elbows flared) and adduction (negative) per arm, taken as constant over the range: Lategan's means for men, 93 ± 27 and 92 ± 23 Nm (isokinetic, 60°/s). Lying on the back, gravity helps abduction and resists adduction in that test and wasn't corrected for, so abduction may read slightly high and adduction slightly low. Weir et al. (via Lategan) found 68 and 74 Nm in 16–18-year-old wrestlers at 30°/s.
strength.source: Lategan L (2002). Normative isokinetic torque values for rehabilitation in South Africa. DPhil thesis, University of Pretoria, Table 6.17 (103 men aged 16–29, isokinetic 60°/s, concentric, lying on the back with the arm out at 90°, not gravity-corrected). https://repository.up.ac.za/handle/2263/27346

strength.note: Shoulder external (positive) and internal (negative) rotation peak torque per arm, taken as constant: Mayer's isometric means for men (30 and 43 Nm).
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric)

strength.note: Relative isometric elbow-flexion torque vs elbow flexion (0° = straight), peak about 95°: the paper's mean cubic fit, normalised, inside the measured 32–120° (held flat beyond). Measured with the upper arm raised 90° and horizontally adducted 20°, not hanging as in a standing curl. Peak per arm: the paper's male means (flexion 85 Nm, extension 77 Nm).
strength.source: Pinter IJ, Bobbert MF, van Soest AJ, Smeets JBJ (2010). Isometric torque–angle relationships of the elbow flexors and extensors in the transverse plane. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 20:923–931. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2010.05.001

strength.note: No muscle capacity: the elbow's sideways moment is carried mostly by ligaments and the joint surfaces, so it is shown as torque only.
strength.source: Not applicable: carried by ligaments and joint surfaces, so no muscle strength is used

strength.note: Relative isometric hip-extension torque vs hip flexion, peak about 53°, measured standing with the knee slightly bent (tested −29° to 74°; deeper hip flexion is held flat at the 74° value, which is extrapolation). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: A typical man's isometric lower-back (L5/S1) extension strength in lifting postures: about 270 N·m, where Tan et al. (295 N·m with the trunk bent 35°), Gallagher (265–270 N·m at 22.5–45°) and Mawston et al. (212–227 N·m in a maximal lift) roughly agree. Upright it is less (Tan et al. 150, Graves et al. 238 N·m). Dolan et al. measured 430 N·m pulling from the floor with the spine flexed (passive tissues add up to 120 N·m fully flexed), and national-level powerlifters reach up to about 990 N·m in deadlifts (Cholewicki et al.), so trained lifters are far stronger: use the strength slider. Taken as the same at every trunk angle (the spine is held neutral). Before 2026-11-05: Graves et al.'s seated machine values (about 238 N·m with the spine neutral), which isolate the back.
strength.source: Tan JC, Parnianpour M, Nordin M, Hofer H, Willems B (1993). Isometric maximal and submaximal trunk extension at different flexed positions in standing. Spine 18(16):2480–2490. doi:10.1097/00007632-199312000-00018 (Fig. 6: 31 men, standing, about L5/S1: about 150, 225 and 295 N·m upright, 15° and 35° bent, read off the figure); Gallagher S (1997). Trunk extension strength and muscle activity in standing and kneeling postures. Spine 22(16):1864–1872. doi:10.1097/00007632-199708150-00011 (Fig. 2: 21 men, standing, isometric medians about 200, 195 and 142 ft·lb, i.e. 270, 265 and 193 N·m, at 22.5°, 45° and 67.5° of trunk flexion, read off the figure); Mawston G, Holder L, O'Sullivan P, Boocock M (2021). Flexed lumbar spine postures are associated with greater strength and efficiency than lordotic postures during a maximal lift in pain-free individuals. Gait Posture 86:245–250. doi:10.1016/j.gaitpost.2021.02.029 (Table 2: 13 men, maximal lift: 212, 217 and 227 N·m with the back arched, mid-range and rounded); range: Dolan P, Mannion AF, Adams MA (1994). Passive tissues help the back muscles to generate extensor moments during lifting. J Biomech 27(8):1077–1085. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(94)90224-0 (Table 1: 23 men, isometric pull from the floor with the lumbar spine 70% flexed: 430 ± 116 N·m; women 245; passive tissues 25 N·m arched to 120 N·m fully flexed); Cholewicki J, McGill SM, Norman RW (1991). Lumbar spine loads during the lifting of extremely heavy weights. Med Sci Sports Exerc 23(10):1179–1186. doi:10.1249/00005768-199110000-00012 (national powerlifting championship deadlifts: L4/L5 moments up to 988 N·m on average for the heaviest lifts)

muscles.name: Latissimus dorsi
muscles.note: Main shoulder extensor: pulls the upper arm back towards the hips. In a row the lats work at about 1.5–2 times the biceps (Lehman et al.: 30–37% vs 18–20% of maximum in seated rows), more than the elbow's torque alone suggests, so here they also follow the elbow's effort (× 1.2).
muscles.source: Lehman GJ, Buchan DD, Lundy A, Myers N, Nalborczyk A (2004). Variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises: an experimental study. Dyn Med 3:4. doi:10.1186/1476-5918-3-4 (Table 1: isometric holds, % of maximum); Di Fonza D, Di Claudio G, Colantuono G, Persichini L, Cerulo N, Sangregorio B, Buonsenso A, Fiorilli G, Calcagno G, di Cagno A (2026). Electromyographic analysis of latissimus dorsi activation during common resistance training exercises: a narrative review. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(3):315. doi:10.3390/jfmk11030315

muscles.name: Posterior deltoid
muscles.note: Horizontal abductor: pulls the upper arm out and back when the elbows flare. With the elbows tucked the lats do that job instead. It works even with the elbows tucked: about 0.75 × the lats' level in a seated row with a close handle (49% against 64% of maximum at an 8-rep maximum: Padovan et al. 2025), the same with a narrow or wide grip (Padovan et al. 2026), so here at least 0.7 × the lats; flaring the elbows raises it further (de Abreu Vasconcelos et al.).
muscles.source: Padovan R, Cè E, Longo S, Tornatore G, Esposito F, Coratella G (2025). High-density surface electromyography excitation of prime movers across scapular positions in the seated row. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):6. doi:10.3390/jfmk11010006 (Fig. 4: 14 trained men, 8-RM, concentric phase, % of maximal isometric activation; values read off the figure); Padovan R, Cè E, Longo S, Tornatore G, Trentin C, Esposito F, Coratella G (2026). High-density surface electromyography excitation of prime movers in the narrow vs. wide grip seated row exercise. J Hum Kinet 104:71–86. doi:10.5114/jhk/209550 (posterior deltoid alike with a narrow and a wide grip); de Abreu Vasconcelos CMW, Lopes CR, Almeida VM, Krause Neto W, Soares E (2023). Effect of different grip position and shoulder-abduction angle on muscle strength and activation during the seated cable row. Int J Strength Cond 3(1). doi:10.47206/ijsc.v3i1.190 (21 adults: posterior deltoid and upper and middle trapezius rise with the elbows out at 60–90°)

muscles.name: Biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis
muscles.note: Elbow flexors: work while the forearm is tilted away from the line of the load. About the same in every row and pulldown variant Lehman et al. tested (15–20% of maximum, isometric holds).
muscles.source: Lehman GJ, Buchan DD, Lundy A, Myers N, Nalborczyk A (2004). Variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises: an experimental study. Dyn Med 3:4. doi:10.1186/1476-5918-3-4 (Table 1: isometric holds, % of maximum)

muscles.name: Rhomboids, middle trapezius
muscles.note: Pull the shoulder blades together at the top. No torque of their own in the model (it has no shoulder blade), so only the measured ratio: the middle trapezius works at about 0.7 × the lats' level in the seated row (47% against 64% of maximum at an 8-rep maximum: Padovan et al. 2025), more with a wide grip or the elbows out (Padovan et al. 2026; de Abreu Vasconcelos et al.). The rhomboids weren't measured; they are taken to work with the middle trapezius.
muscles.source: Padovan R, Cè E, Longo S, Tornatore G, Esposito F, Coratella G (2025). High-density surface electromyography excitation of prime movers across scapular positions in the seated row. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):6. doi:10.3390/jfmk11010006 (Fig. 4: 14 trained men, 8-RM, concentric phase, % of maximal isometric activation; values read off the figure); Padovan R, Cè E, Longo S, Tornatore G, Trentin C, Esposito F, Coratella G (2026). High-density surface electromyography excitation of prime movers in the narrow vs. wide grip seated row exercise. J Hum Kinet 104:71–86. doi:10.5114/jhk/209550 (posterior deltoid alike with a narrow and a wide grip); de Abreu Vasconcelos CMW, Lopes CR, Almeida VM, Krause Neto W, Soares E (2023). Effect of different grip position and shoulder-abduction angle on muscle strength and activation during the seated cable row. Int J Strength Cond 3(1). doi:10.47206/ijsc.v3i1.190 (21 adults: posterior deltoid and upper and middle trapezius rise with the elbows out at 60–90°)

muscles.name: Erector spinae
muscles.note: Hold the trunk still against the cable's pull and, when leaning, its own weight. Driven by the lower back's effort: the moment at L5/S1 of everything above it (trunk, head, arms, the cable's pull), against the measured lumbar extension strength with the spine neutral. Hardest at the start, with the arms reaching forward; none when a pad carries the chest.
muscles.source: Strength: Graves JE, Pollock ML, Carpenter DM, Leggett SH, Jones A, MacMillan M, Fulton M (1990). Quantitative assessment of full range-of-motion isometric lumbar extension strength. Spine 15(4):289–294. doi:10.1097/00007632-199004000-00008 (Fig. 4: 56 men, MedX machine, seated, pelvis and femurs restrained, torso weight counterbalanced)

muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.note: With the glutes, hold the hip angle against the cable pulling the trunk forward.

muscles.name: Infraspinatus, teres minor
muscles.note: External rotators of the rotator cuff: hold the upper arm from turning inwards. In a row the infraspinatus is nearly silent (3% of maximum at 70% of the 1RM, the lats 74%: Wattanaprakornkul et al.), so here at least 0.05 × the lats.
muscles.source: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA (2011). Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 21(6):1041–1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002 (Fig. 5A: 15 adults, fine-wire electrodes in the cuff, seated machine press and row at 20, 50 and 70% of maximum load, % of maximal isometric activation; values read off the figure)

muscles.name: Subscapularis
muscles.note: Internal rotator of the rotator cuff: holds the humeral head forward against the lats' backward pull, and the upper arm from turning outwards. EMG (Wattanaprakornkul et al.): 32% of maximum against the lats' 74% at 70% of the 1RM (20% against 56% at 50%), so here at least 0.4 × the lats.
muscles.source: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA (2011). Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 21(6):1041–1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002 (Fig. 5A: 15 adults, fine-wire electrodes in the cuff, seated machine press and row at 20, 50 and 70% of maximum load, % of maximal isometric activation; values read off the figure)

muscles.name: Supraspinatus
muscles.note: Keeps the head of the humerus centred in the socket. In the row it works at about a sixth of the lats' level (12% of maximum against 74% at 70% of the 1RM, 9% against 56% at 50%: Wattanaprakornkul et al.), so here 0.16 × the lats. The model has no supraspinatus torque of its own: the ratio is all it has.
muscles.source: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA (2011). Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 21(6):1041–1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002 (Fig. 5A: 15 adults, fine-wire electrodes in the cuff, seated machine press and row at 20, 50 and 70% of maximum load, % of maximal isometric activation; values read off the figure)

variants.name: Seated cable row, trunk upright
variants.notes: Trunk held upright, handle pulled to the belly. The cable pulls the trunk forward, so the hips and lower back hold it, most at the start, when the hands are far out in front and high above the hips. Close-grip (V) handle: the hands sit near the middle, so the cables pull the arms slightly inwards. The hands move in a straight line; elbows tucked in the side view's plane. Stack weight only: the machine's pulley friction is ignored.

variants.name: Leaning back 15°
variants.notes: Trunk leaning back: the body's weight behind the hips now counters the cable, so the hips and lower back do less. Leaning back during the pull (body English) uses this to shift work away from the arms. Close-grip (V) handle: the hands sit near the middle, so the cables pull the arms slightly inwards. The hands move in a straight line; elbows tucked in the side view's plane. Stack weight only: the machine's pulley friction is ignored.

variants.name: Leaning forward 20°
variants.notes: Trunk leaning towards the stack: both the trunk's weight and the cable now pull forward, so the hips and lower back work hardest. The lats pull through a longer arc. Close-grip (V) handle: the hands sit near the middle, so the cables pull the arms slightly inwards. The hands move in a straight line; elbows tucked in the side view's plane. Stack weight only: the machine's pulley friction is ignored.

variants.name: Chest-supported dumbbell row
variants.notes: Chest on an incline pad, trunk 50° from vertical, dumbbells hanging. The pad carries the trunk, so the lower back is out of it: the arms and upper back do all the work. Load = both dumbbells together. The hands move in a straight line; elbows tucked in the side view's plane.

variants.name: Wide bar, elbows out
variants.equipment: Cable, long bar, seat and foot plate
variants.notes: Long bar held wide, elbows flared about 70°, pulled to the lower chest: the rear delts and upper back do much more of the work, the lats and biceps less. Stack weight only; pulley friction ignored.

phases.name: Reach
phases.text: Arms long: the cable (or the dumbbells) pulls on straight arms; the trunk holds the load.

phases.name: Pull
phases.text: Elbows bend and travel back: the elbow flexors and lats share the work.

phases.name: Squeeze
phases.text: Hands at the trunk, elbows behind it: the lats do most of the work, and the shoulder blades squeeze together.

wger.name: Seated Cable Row
wger.note: Checked against wger's public exercise list (id = the number in the page address). Closest entry: no exact "Seated Cable Rows"; alternative 1725 "Seated Row (Machine)".

momentArmNote: Moment arm = the joint's 3D distance from the load's line of action through that hand (the cable, or straight down); it feeds every component of that joint's torque.

placement.label: Grip: each hand from the middle
Elbows out from the trunk (0 = tucked)
Shoulder blades: reach forward → squeeze back (travel)
